opening_summary: Thirty-four ideas, each with its name in Godot, Unity and Unreal, from scenes and signals to clocks, collision, units and licences. Knowing each engine's exact word lets you port a game idea and instruct an agent precisely.
opening_description: 34 terms mapped across Godot, Unity and Unreal.

idea.narration: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. People moving from Godot to Unity often say a node is a component. Not quite. A Godot node is one object, like a Unity GameObject. Where Unity adds components, Godot uses a node type and child nodes. The Unity and Unreal names come from their documentation, not from runs. This film goes through the terms, each one shown with all three names.
idea.text:
A Godot node is
a Unity component.
idea.replacementWords: one object, like a Unity GameObject

beats.narration: This table is the map. Thirty-four terms, each one idea with three engine names, Godot, Unity and Unreal. The first group is what things are called. Scene, node, component, template, instance, override and data asset. These are the building blocks, and how copies relate.

The second group is how code runs and talks. Signal, UnityEvent, Event Dispatcher and autoload, then the languages, GDScript, C sharp, Blueprint and C plus plus, and the clocks. These terms cover languages, loops and messages.

The third group is how things move and touch. Input action, character body, trigger, layer and mask, Collision Matrix and Object Type. These terms say how input arrives, what moves a body, and who notices whom.
The fourth group is space, looks and shipping. Up axis, units, clip, event key, state machine, shader, parameter, particles, export and licence. Axes, animation, materials, and the build you ship.

A table with a column for each engine, filling one row at a time. The first row is Scene, Level, Map. A Godot scene, a Unity Scene and an Unreal Level are each a saved, reusable tree of objects, and Unreal calls its level file a Map. A level is narrower, one playable space. For example, in Godot the first level of a platformer is a scene file, and so is the coin placed in it, but only the first is a level.

The second row is Node, GameObject, Actor, the name for one object in the scene. A node is Godot's object, and each node type already does one job. A Unity GameObject does nothing until components are added, and an Unreal Actor also gains its behaviour from components. For example, the player of a platformer is one CharacterBody2D node in Godot, one GameObject in Unity, and one Actor in Unreal.

The third row is Component, a piece of behaviour or data attached to a GameObject or an Actor. Godot has no component here. It picks a node type, and adds child nodes, instead. For example, a coin pickup in Unity is a GameObject with a collider component added and set as a trigger. In Godot the same coin is an Area2D node, with its collision shape as a child node.

Now the same player, drawn three ways. Red is the object itself. In Godot it is three nodes, one root and two filled child nodes. In Unity it is one GameObject with three outlined components, and in Unreal one Actor with three components. The idea is the same, and the shape is not. For example, when you ask an agent to port that player to Unity, ask for components on one GameObject, not a tree of child nodes.

A single box at the top holds a speed of one hundred sixty. A Template is the master that copies come from. In Godot it is a scene, in Unity a Prefab, and in Unreal a Blueprint class. Edit the template, and the copies follow. For example, an enemy saved once as a template, with its patrol speed inside, can be placed all over a level, and every copy starts from that saved speed.

Five boxes appear below it, each a copy holding one hundred sixty. An Instance is one copy made from a template and placed in the game. Edit an instance, and only that copy changes. In Unity it is called a prefab instance. For example, the five enemies in your level are five instances of the one enemy template, so each can stand in its own spot with its own position.

The template's speed changes to one hundred ninety-two, and four copies follow. Copy three keeps two hundred, because it holds an Override, a change made on one instance. In Unity, Apply pushes an override back into the Prefab, and Revert drops it. For example, you make one guard at a castle gate faster than the rest. If you later want every guard that fast, you press Apply on that guard.

Now one asset with three readers. A Data asset is shared data kept as a file in the project, not in a scene. Godot calls it a Resource, Unity a ScriptableObject, and Unreal a Data Asset. Here a Player, a Bot and a Menu take their speed from it, and one edit updates all three. For example, Walker keeps its run speed in a tuning resource, and a Unity version would keep it in a ScriptableObject asset.

A ball exits, and lines run to two listeners, Score and Sound. A Signal is Godot's named event. Other nodes connect to it and run when it fires. Here it fires once, and both listeners get the call, two of two. For example, in a Pong game the ball exited signal fires when the ball leaves the court, and the score counter and the goal sound both answer it.

The same ball exit in Unity, now with three listeners. Unity's events are the UnityEvent and the C sharp event. A UnityEvent can be wired in the Inspector, the editor panel, so that listener is stored in the scene file and not in any script. Here the UI listener was wired that way, three of three. For example, an agent that checks only the scripts of your Unity port can miss that the score text listens at all.

Now Unreal. An Event Dispatcher is Unreal's Blueprint form of a signal. You bind events to it, and one Call fires every bound event. In C plus plus the same job is done by a delegate. Here Sound was bound twice, so its handler runs twice, three calls in all. For example, a coin whose sound handler was bound twice would play its pickup sound twice on a single touch.

A new scene loads, and six objects face it. Autoload, Game Instance names the things that outlive a scene. Godot uses an autoload, Unity calls DontDestroyOnLoad on a root object, and Unreal uses the Game Instance, or a subsystem that shares its lifetime. The score keeper and the music are kept, two of six. A signal is an announcement, and an autoload is what is kept across scene changes. For example, music that keeps playing from the menu into the first level needs one.

Lanes from edit to run, one per language. GDScript is Godot's own scripting language, and its scripts are plain text files. Its lane has two stages, edit and run, because a change takes effect the next time Godot runs. Plain text also gives a diff, the lines that changed. For example, when an agent changes the jump height in a player script, you see the exact line in the diff and run the game straight away.

C sharp is Unity's language, and a MonoBehaviour is a component script, also plain text. Its lane adds a compile stage, three in all. Compile means turning code into a runnable form, which is not the same as a diff, the lines that changed. For example, a Unity port of a coin script would be a MonoBehaviour on the coin's GameObject. You can diff it as text, but it must compile before the change runs.

A Blueprint graph is Unreal's visual scripting, boxes joined by wires. The graph is saved as a binary asset, so an agent cannot diff it as text. Its lane has three stages, with compile in the middle, and it is marked binary. For example, if the run speed lives on a Blueprint character, an agent cannot change it by editing a file. It has to work through the editor, and you check the change in the editor's own diff tool.

C plus plus in Unreal is the code route. It is plain text, so it gives a text diff, but it must be compiled before a change takes effect, three stages again. That makes each try slower than in GDScript. For example, an agent can set the player's default run speed in a C plus plus constructor and show you the diff, and then the project is compiled before you can test the new speed.

Strips of tick marks across one second, on a screen that draws a frame one hundred forty-four times a second. In Godot, the process function runs once per frame, so here one hundred forty-four times. The physics process function runs at a fixed sixty times a second by default, the red marks, sixteen point seven milliseconds apart. For example, a coin's spin can go in the process function, while the player's run and jump belong in the physics process function.

Unity has the same two clocks under other names. Update runs once per frame, so the gap between calls can be any length. FixedUpdate runs at fixed steps of zero point zero two seconds, which is fifty a second by default, not sixty. For example, a test of a jump ported to Unity that counts physics steps over one second must expect fifty steps, not the sixty it counted in Godot.

In Unreal, Tick is the per-frame update. Each Actor ticks every frame, so both lower strips show one hundred forty-four ticks in the second. Tick groups, such as pre-physics and post-physics, order that work around the physics step. For example, an enemy Actor's per-frame logic runs in its Tick, and placing it in the pre-physics group makes it run before the physics step in each frame.

Three rows of key presses, one per engine. An Input action is a named intent, such as jump, bound to keys or buttons and kept apart from them. Godot keeps it in the InputMap, Unity in the Input System, and Unreal in Enhanced Input. Space and a gamepad button are bound and Enter is not, so jump fires on three of four presses. For example, porting Walker's jump means binding Space to a jump action, not testing the Space key in code.

A Character body is the body you move on purpose. In Godot it is a CharacterBody2D that your script moves with move and slide, in Unity a Rigidbody2D stepped in FixedUpdate, and in Unreal a Character whose movement component does the moving. Each dot covers one hundred sixty pixels in one second, in sixty, fifty or one hundred forty-four steps. For example, Walker's player is a CharacterBody2D, and in Unreal its run speed would become the movement component's max walk speed.

A Trigger is a zone that reports overlaps instead of blocking, which a collider does. Godot uses an Area2D, Unity a collider with Is Trigger ticked, and Unreal a Trigger volume. The dot crosses the zone in one second, and each engine reports the entry once. Unity also needs a Rigidbody2D on one of the two objects, and Unreal needs Generate Overlap Events on both. For example, Walker's goal flag is an Area2D that notices the player without stopping it.

A grid in which each row notices each column. Layer and mask is Godot's rule. Each object has a layer, where it sits, and a mask, what it looks for. One object notices another if the other's layer is in its mask, and that works one way. Here the Player's mask holds Mob and Coin, and they mask nothing, so two of six pairs notice. For example, in a dodge game the player detects the mobs while the mobs detect nothing.

Unity uses a Layer Collision Matrix. Each GameObject sits on one layer, and one grid for the whole project says which pairs of layers collide. A tick works both ways, so ticking Player with Mob and Player with Coin makes four of six pairs notice. For example, the dodge game's setup, where the player detects mobs that detect nothing, becomes a matrix setting in Unity, shared by every object on those layers.

Unreal gives each object an Object Type and a response, Block, Overlap or Ignore, for every other type. Both sides must agree before contact happens. A mask is one side's filter, and a response needs both. Here the Mob answers Ignore and does not generate overlap events, so the Player meets the Mob with no event, and no error. For example, if the creep in an Unreal shield pickup game forgot Generate Overlap Events, the shield check would silently stop working.

Three axis drawings, one per engine, with the up axis in red. The up axis is the one that points up. Godot and Unity are Y-up, so height is the y value, and Unreal is Z-up, so height is the z value. Handedness is the other half of the setup. Unity and Unreal are left-handed, and Godot is right-handed. For example, in a three D game, a jump that raises the player's y value in Godot raises its z value in Unreal.

The same post, three metres ahead and one point eight metres up, on two charts. In Unity it sits at zero, one point eight, three, in metres. In Unreal it sits at three hundred, zero, one hundred eighty, in centimetres. The map takes X from z, Y from x and Z from y, then multiplies by one hundred. For example, a checkpoint flag placed in a Unity level needs exactly this conversion before its position means anything in Unreal.

Units says how long one unit of distance is. In Godot and Unity one unit is one metre. In Unreal one unit is one centimetre. So the same post is one point eight on one ruler and one hundred eighty on the other. The importer converts, but your expected numbers must change too. For example, a test that checks a doorway is one point eight high now expects one hundred eighty, and a tolerance of zero point zero five metres becomes five.

Three timelines, one per engine, each playing a clip half a second long. A clip is keyed data played over time, a value that changes from key to key, and a player runs it. Godot uses an AnimationPlayer with an Animation, Unity an Animator with an Animation Clip, and Unreal an Animation Sequence. Unity wraps even one clip in an Animator Controller. For example, a coin's half-second bounce would be one clip in each engine.

Keys now sit at zero point one and zero point two five seconds. An Event key is a call placed on the timeline, a method track in Godot, an Animation Event in Unity, and a Notify in Unreal, which fires at one time. An Anim Notify State, the red window, has a begin and an end. The hitbox stays on zero point one five seconds, nine steps at sixty hertz, eight at fifty. For example, a sword swing switches its hitbox on and off this way.

Three boxes joined by arrows, Idle, Walk and Attack. A State machine is a set of states joined by transitions with rules, and the current state picks the clip. Here a speed above zero point one moves Idle to Walk, attack moves Walk to Attack, and attack finished returns to Idle. Godot builds it in an AnimationTree, Unity in an Animator Controller, and Unreal in an Anim Blueprint. For example, a player sprite that plays its walk clip only while moving is driven by one.

Where each engine defines how a surface looks. A shader is code that draws, and a material holds the settings it reads. Godot and Unity write shaders as code or as a graph. Unreal builds materials as node graphs in the Material Editor, with a Custom node for HLSL, the high level shading language. Unreal's material is a binary asset, and the other two can be plain text. For example, a flash shader on a Godot sprite is a text file an agent can edit.

One flash value is set from code in each engine, and the swatches fade to grey as it falls to zero. A Material parameter is a named value that your code sets and the shader reads. Godot calls it a uniform, set on a ShaderMaterial. Unity sets a material property, or a MaterialPropertyBlock for one object. Unreal sets a scalar parameter on a Dynamic Material Instance. For example, an enemy that flashes when hit sets its flash value high, then lets it fall.

In this seeded simulation, thirty-two particles burst from one point. A Particle system is many small sprites simulated together. Godot uses GPUParticles, Unity the VFX Graph, and Unreal Niagara. A one-shot burst spawns them all at once, and with one shared lifetime of zero point six seconds, all thirty-two end together. For example, the sparks when the player grabs a coin can be a one-shot burst that plays once and is gone.

Three build commands, typed out. Build and export means packaging the project for a platform. Godot saves export presets and needs one flag on the editor. Unity six saves a build profile, and your script calls its build pipeline. Unreal packages the project and cooks it, converting every asset for the target, so export and cook are different steps. For example, shipping your platformer for the web from Godot starts from a saved web export preset.

Licence means the terms you build and sell under. Godot is MIT licensed, with no royalty. Unity is proprietary, and its Personal plan holds only while twelve-month finances stay at or under two hundred thousand dollars. Unreal is source-available, not open source, with a five percent royalty above the first million dollars per product. For example, in this illustrative case a game grosses one and a half million dollars, and owes nothing under Godot and twenty-five thousand dollars under Unreal.
Each pair sets two look-alike ideas side by side. Edit the template, and every copy without an override changes, three of three. Edit an instance, and only that copy changes, one of three.
Y-up against Z-up. In Godot and Unity, height is y, in metres, so the dot rises to one point eight. In Unreal, height is z, in centimetres, so the same dot rises to one hundred eighty.

Update against FixedUpdate. Update runs once per frame, so the gaps vary, thirty-nine frames in a quarter second here. FixedUpdate runs every zero point zero two seconds in Unity, however many frames pass, thirteen steps.

A Godot mask against an Unreal response. In Godot, one object notices another when the other's layer is in its mask, so one side decides. In Unreal, both sides must answer Overlap or Block. Here the second object says Ignore, so nothing happens.

Each vague request becomes an exact instruction. Convert it for Unreal becomes, map the Unity point with X from z, Y from x and Z from y, times one hundred. The answer is three hundred, zero, one hundred eighty. Y is zero, so the post is straight ahead.

Run it at the right rate becomes, Godot runs physics sixty times a second and Unity's FixedUpdate fifty, so count steps. That is sixteen point seven milliseconds a step against twenty, and ten fewer steps a second in Unity.
Make the pickup fire becomes, in Unity tick Is Trigger and give one of the two objects a Rigidbody2D. Of the four combinations of those two settings, only one fires, the one with both.
Make the mob see the player becomes, in Unreal both Actors answer Overlap and turn on Generate Overlap Events. Again only one of four settings fires, overlap yes and events on yes.
Update every enemy becomes, edit the template. Four of five copies change to one hundred ninety-two, and the one with an override keeps its two hundred. An override beats the template.
A checklist of six questions to ask before you port an idea between engines. First, am I using this engine's word, node, GameObject or Actor?
Second, which clock does the code need. Per frame, or the fixed step, sixty a second in Godot and fifty in Unity?
figures: 60 a second in Godot, 50 in Unity

beats.narration: Third, which way is up, y or z, and are the units metres or centimetres? Get either one wrong and every position in the level is off.
Fourth, does contact work from one side, as with a Godot mask, or do both sides have to agree, as with an Unreal response?
Fifth, is the asset text that you can diff, like a Godot scene or a C sharp script, or binary, like a Blueprint, that you must open the editor for?

Sixth, was it run, or only looked up in documentation? Neither Unity nor Unreal was run for these comparisons. Then say it exactly. Not make it work in Unity, but tick Is Trigger and add a Rigidbody2D.

recap_lines: A Godot node maps to a Unity GameObject and an Unreal Actor.
Edit the template and copies follow, but an override keeps its own value.
A Blueprint graph is binary, so an agent cannot diff it as text.
Godot's fixed step runs sixty times a second, Unity's FixedUpdate fifty.
A Godot mask works one way, and an Unreal response needs both sides.
Godot and Unity are Y-up in metres, and Unreal is Z-up in centimetres.

your_turn.segment: Name The Term In Each Engine
your_turn.command: Quiz me on porting a Godot game to Unity and Unreal, with short game-making cases, one at a time. Use the terms GameObject, Actor, Prefab, override, ScriptableObject, Event Dispatcher, FixedUpdate, Layer Collision Matrix, Object Type and Z-up. For each case I must name the exact term in the right engine and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply.
checks: Check: each case names the engine, and the answer waits for your reply.
Check: you gave the exact engine term and said why the look-alike fails.

deck_problems: Slide 10 (Animation: clip, event key, state machine), step 3: the final readout is 'speed = 0.8 attack = off state = Idle', but the drawn rule sends Idle to Walk when speed > 0.1. In renderAnim the speed stays 0.8 after 'attack finished' returns the state to Idle, so the last frame breaks the slide's own rule. No Walk-to-Idle transition is drawn either. The narration describes the transitions and does not speak 0.8.

Slide 7 step 3: 'Godot: area_entered 1' for a BODY crossing the zone. In Godot a body entering an Area2D emits body_entered; area_entered is for another area. Chapter 4's Unity table pairs Area2D + body_entered with OnTriggerEnter2D. The narration does not name the signal.

Slide 12 step 2: 'Personal plan: not available' compares a lifetime gross of US$1,500,000 with Unity's twelve-month finance threshold of US$200,000, two different bases. The step also sits under the badge 'Computed' while its revenue figure is labelled ILLUSTRATIVE. The narration says illustrative and does not speak the Unity verdict.
Slide 11: the badge 'Simulation (seeded)' covers steps 1 and 2, which show where shaders live and a parameter call, not a simulation.

Slide 4 step 3: Unreal's 'Sound' and 'Sound (bound twice)' are drawn as two separate listener boxes, so the picture reads as three listeners rather than one listener bound twice; 'Calls received: 3 of 3' reinforces that.
Slide 9 step 1: the three axis gizmos are drawn identically (two axes each), so handedness, which the step names, cannot be seen in the picture; only the labels differ.

Slide 13 pair 3: '39 frames in 0.25 s' comes from randomly jittered frame gaps; at the 144 frames a second used on slide 6, a quarter second holds 36 frames. '13 steps in 0.25 s' counts the tick at time zero (0.25 / 0.02 = 12.5).

Slide 7 step 2: 'Character body' is defined as 'the body you move on purpose', but its Unity column, Rigidbody2D, can be dynamic (moved by physics); Chapter 1 gives 'Rigidbody2D (kinematic or dynamic)'.

Map names differ from the slide entries: 'Collision Matrix' vs 'Layer Collision Matrix', 'Object Type' vs 'Object Type, response', 'Blueprint' vs 'Blueprint graph', 'C#' vs 'C# and MonoBehaviour', 'Shader', 'Parameter', 'Particles', 'Export' vs 'Shader and material', 'Material parameter', 'Particle system', 'Build and export'. Group 2 lists nine names for eleven terms because 'the clocks' stands for three entries.
Title slide note says 'Deck 12 of the topic order' while the file is deck 23.
